ops.detail: Pulled out of a sample message reading "need a proposal by Friday". Speed becomes a correctness property, not a nice-to-have.

ops.label: A prompt improves the answer; a bot improves its arrival
ops.detail: This is the whole justification for reaching for a chatbot here instead of better prompting. Everything in the module before this optimised for accuracy — this lecture moves the goalpost to delivery.

ops.label: Three properties that make inbound queries worth automating
It repeats — a small set of questions covers most of the volume
ops.detail: Repetition is what lets the answer be pre-written. In the case study the recurring set is refund policy, pricing, seasonality and permits.

ops.label: It is scattered — several channels, no single inbox
ops.detail: Scatter means no human is watching everywhere at once. Case study: Instagram DMs, WhatsApp, a website form and Gmail.

ops.label: It arrives off-hours — the gap is structural, not a staffing failure
ops.detail: Nobody is awake when the question lands, and no amount of hiring fixes a question that arrives when the business is closed.

ops.markdown:
**The bot does not have to answer everything.**

It has to absorb the recurring majority plus the obvious cases, and hand the rest to a human.

This is a design constraint, not a limitation to apologise for. Aiming at total coverage is what produces a bot that invents answers at the edges — which is the exact failure the Dify section spends 25 minutes on.

cells.c-what: Small travel agency, Jaipur, founded 2021. Sells tour plans and tickets — the mediator, like a Cleartrip or Goibibo
Founder. Eleven years on a hotel front desk. Knows travel cold, knows tech not at all
"This is us." Marketing intern who became the laptop guy by default. Has never written a line of code — which is why all three tools are no-code
The two travel consultants, on phones and WhatsApp all day. They are the ones who actually close deals
Seasonal bench across Ladakh, Spiti, Rajasthan, Kerala. Re-briefed from scratch every March — this is the problem Voiceflow shows up to solve
312 queries a week, four channels, 71% of them one of six questions, most arriving after midnight
The company and its documents are AI-generated props — the instructor says so on air. None of these numbers are real data; they are teaching material

ops.title: The dial — who decides what happens next

ops.label: Dify — knowledge-linked app builder
ops.detail: "You supply documents + instructions. The model composes every reply." Fastest to a working FAQ bot.

ops.label: Botpress — open-source flow builder
ops.detail: "You draw the flow and decide which branches the model is allowed to run." Both hands on the wheel.

ops.label: Voiceflow — conversation design tool
ops.detail: "The conversation is designed, reviewed and signed off before it is built." Built for teams, voice and CX.

ops.markdown:
> All three ship a working chatbot. None of them is "the good one."
> **The skill is matching the shape of the tool to the shape of the risk.**

The choice is not a capability comparison — it is a risk assessment. Look at what a single wrong sentence would cost you, and pick the tool whose shape absorbs that cost.

ops.label: Getting from A to B in your city
Dify — give the driver the address and go to sleep
ops.detail: A local driver of fifteen years. You wake up at the destination. You don't know the route, the time or the petrol — only that you arrived. No control, and the process is a black box.

ops.label: Botpress — hand the driver a route map
ops.detail: First left, second right, straight at the roundabout. The driver still drives — you are not steering — but you decided the path.

ops.label: Voiceflow — the family approves the route before the driver gets it
ops.detail: Your brother says no, your sister proposes a different turn, the route goes back for rework. Only the signed-off version reaches the driver.

ops.label: In all three, the driver still drives
ops.detail: What moves along the dial is not how much AI is involved — the model generates in every one of them. What moves is how much of the route was decided before the model got the wheel.

ops.title: Why reliability improves along the dial

ops.label: Hallucination risk falls as you move right
The mechanism is surface area, not a better model
ops.detail: Same models underneath all three. Every sentence the model is allowed to generate is a sentence that can come out wrong — so removing generation from a branch removes the chance of a new failure there. You don't make the model more reliable; you give it fewer chances to be unreliable.

ops.label: Dify can hallucinate — every reply is composed fresh
Botpress reduces it because you supplied the route
Voiceflow's review is a design-time check, not a runtime one
ops.detail: A different kind of reduction. Botpress reduces what the model can say at runtime; Voiceflow catches bad design before the bot ships at all.

ops.title: Dify — what it is, and what it isn't

ops.label: Open-source platform for building LLM apps without code
Pick a model, write instructions, attach a knowledge base, publish
ops.detail: Publishes as a hosted web app, an embeddable widget, or an API.

ops.label: Their cloud or self-hosted on your own server
ops.detail: This is the answer when a client says the word "data". Self-hosting keeps the conversation alive where a pure SaaS proposal dies on the spot.

ops.label: Not an LLM — a wrapper over Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and others
ops.detail: It makes the model call and does extra work around it. You still bring a model.

ops.label: Not an agent — a tool for building agents
ops.detail: Matters when someone asks what you built: you built an agent, using Dify.

ops.label: User query
Search the knowledge base
ops.detail: This half is retrieval — finding the material that bears on the question.

ops.label: KB documents — chunked on upload, stored as embeddings
User prompt = query + retrieved material
ops.detail: This half is augmentation — inserting the retrieved material into the prompt alongside the query. This combined prompt is what the model actually answers from.

ops.label: Generate LLM output

ops.title: RAG is the technique, not the differentiator

ops.markdown:
All three tools chunk your documents on upload and retrieve against them. **RAG is not what separates them** — which is why the dial is drawn on control rather than on retrieval.

> "RAG is a technique. I am walking, walking is a technique — but me walking, you walking, or him walking are three different people."

A student asked whether *query + file* differs from *chunks + query*. It doesn't — the file in the diagram is shorthand for the retrieved chunks of it, not the whole PDF going into the prompt.

Useful against a vendor pitch: "we use RAG" names the technique and says nothing about how good the retrieval is.

cells.c-cont: Ladakh 6D/5N, Spiti 7D/6N, Rajasthan circuit, Kerala backwaters — inclusions, exclusions, per-person pricing
The tiered slab — the object the whole lecture turns on
Best months per circuit, road-closure windows, altitude advisories
Inner-line permits for Ladakh; what the agency does and explicitly does not do on visas

ops.markdown:
All four documents **already existed on the founder's laptop**. Nothing was written for the bot — which is exactly why this use case is so common in the real world.

The folder on screen actually held six files (a commission policy and a guide handbook as well); four were uploaded. The KB was a deliberate selection, not a folder dump.

Shared with the class here — the input for the break exercise and the doubt-session assignment:

[Wanderline knowledge base (Google Drive)](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1N8wBxnrVi_mRSUdC2nBX6wHtppG3e76r)

```
You are the enquiry assistant for Wanderline Travel, a small
travel agency based in Jaipur, India.

YOUR JOB
Answer traveller questions about Wanderline's trips using ONLY
the retrieved context from the knowledge base.

HARD RULES
1. If the answer is not in the retrieved context, say exactly:
   "I don't have that detail — let me get Divya to confirm."
   Then ask for their name and phone number.
2. Never invent a price, a date, a refund percentage, or a
   permit requirement. Not even an approximate one.
3. Never give visa advice beyond what the Visa & Permits FAQ says.
4. If someone sounds distressed, stuck, or is describing a
   problem with a trip already in progress — do not try to
   solve it. Say: "I'm getting a human on this right now."

STYLE
Warm, brief, plain English. Two to four sentences.
No emoji. Never say "as an AI."
Always end an answer with one relevant follow-up question.

ALWAYS CAPTURE
Before the conversation ends, get: travel month, number of
travellers, and one contact detail.
```

cells.c-block: "You are the enquiry assistant… Jaipur, India"
ALWAYS CAPTURE — the framework was built for answering; this prompt has a commercial job on top of answering

ops.label: Every block is defending against a specific failure
"Using ONLY the retrieved context" — grounding stated as a rule
ops.detail: Pairs with turning web grounding off in the LLM node. One is instruction, the other is configuration, and you want both — an instruction on its own can be talked past.

ops.label: The refusal is specified down to the exact sentence
ops.detail: Not "say you don't know" but say exactly this string. A refusal the model composes freely can drift into a guess.

ops.label: …and the refusal is followed by asking for name and number
ops.detail: The failure to answer is converted into a captured lead. The bot's worst case is still commercially useful.

ops.label: Escalation triggers on emotional state, not on topic
ops.detail: Distressed, stuck, or mid-trip — none of those are subject matter. When a person is upset, correctness stops being the goal and speed to a human is. Botpress rebuilds this as a hard branch, which is the argument for the second tool.

ops.label: The ceiling: all of this is instruction, and compliance is optional
ops.detail: In the failure that follows, the model obeys the refusal rule while blurring the never-invent rule — it does not invent a refund percentage, it vaguely paraphrases the real one. The prompt says don't invent. It does not say don't blur.

ops.label: User input
ops.detail: Studio → Create from blank → Chat flow. Name it; the description is optional and capped around 400 characters.

ops.label: Knowledge Retrieval node
ops.detail:
Query text ← user_input.query. Attach the knowledge base — all four files arrive as one selection. Output is `result`.

Uploading the KB: Home → Knowledge → create → Import from file. One file at a time on the free tier; batch upload is a paid unlock. Leave max chunk size, delimiter, chunk overlap and top-K score threshold at defaults.

ops.label: LLM node
ops.detail:
Pick the model. Temperature low (0.2–0.3). Grounding off, URL context off, code execution off.

Context wiring: select knowledge_retrieval.result in the Context field AND reference it inside the prompt body with {{ }}.

ops.label: Answer node
ops.detail:
Must be {{ LLM.text }}. Leave plain text there and it returns that literal string forever.

Publish → Access point for the web-app URL, or Embed into site for an iframe that renders as a bottom-corner pop-up.

ops.markdown:
**Temperature low (0.2–0.3).** "Internal data should not hallucinate." Grounded retrieval and high temperature are **contradictory settings** — the point of retrieval is that the answer is determined by the documents, and temperature is the dial that lets the model wander away from what is determined.

**Grounding off, URL context off, code execution off.** This is the configuration half of what the system prompt already said in words. The prompt asks for "only the retrieved context"; these switches make the open web unreachable.

You want both, because one is a request and the other is a wall.

ops.label: 25 minutes lost to a wire between two working nodes
Symptom: the bot refused to answer while citing the document it was refusing to read
ops.detail: It kept firing the hard-rule fallback — "I don't have that detail, let me get Divya to confirm" — and emitted a citation to the very file that held the answer.

ops.label: The contradiction is the diagnosis — the break is between the stages, not inside either
ops.detail: The citation proves retrieval worked. The refusal proves generation saw nothing. Both nodes were fine; the fault was in the wire between them.

ops.label: Fix: selecting the variable in the Context field is not enough — reference it in the prompt body with {{ }}
ops.detail: Supplied by a student in chat and confirmed on air. Otherwise Dify warns you and silently sends nothing.

ops.label: Declaring a variable is not interpolating it
ops.detail: The Context field declares what is available; the {{ }} in the body is what actually puts it into the string sent to the model. Declare without referencing and the model receives a prompt with no documents in it — and correctly answers "I don't have that detail", exactly as instructed.

ops.title: Two takeaways from a failed demo

ops.markdown:
**Getting stuck is the process, not a sign you are bad at it.**

> "These tools do upgrade and change quite frequently, so there is a very high chance we'll get stuck somewhere or the other on some tool, debug it, figure a way out. That's a process all of us will have to get accustomed to."

**Debugging on a pro model is the fastest way to burn a free tier.** Every Preview click is a paid model call, and debugging means clicking Preview many times. His credits ran out mid-demo; the sharper note was that running a *pro* model rather than a *flash* one is what drained them.

*(The specific model names in this stretch are unreliable — partly transcription, partly him switching models mid-build. The pro-vs-flash point stands regardless.)*

ops.label: "List all packages" returned one of four
Retrieval worked. Generation decided one was good enough
ops.detail: The documents were retrieved and were in the prompt. The model made an editorial choice about how much of them to use.

ops.label: A different failure class from the wiring bug
ops.detail: The wiring bug was a break you could find and fix. This is the system working as designed.

ops.label: There is no setting for "use all of it"
ops.detail: The thing deciding is the generation step, and generation is where your control ended. You do not control the output.

ops.markdown:
> **Divya → team group, 9:20 AM · Thursday**
> "The bot told Mr. Raghavan he'd get *'most of his money back'* on a 12-day-out cancellation. The actual slab for under 15 days is 25%. He's screenshotted it. He's quoting it back at me."

**This is not hallucination.** Retrieval worked, the model had the right document with the right number in it, and nothing was invented. Filing it under hallucination sends you after the wrong fix — better grounding, a bigger KB, a stricter threshold — none of which is the problem.

**It paraphrased a binding number into a vague quantifier.** "Most of his money" — 50%? 75%? The real figure was 25%, which is not *most* of anything. And the model was obeying its instructions: the rule said never invent a refund percentage, so it stated none and reached for natural language instead. **The prompt banned invention. It did not ban vagueness.**

**The customer screenshotted it.** That is the move from a technical fault to a liability — a wrong sentence being quoted back at your consultant is a commitment someone will argue you into honouring. Same shape as the Air Canada bereavement-fare case.

The lesson is not that models make mistakes. It is that **the cost of a wrong sentence is not spread evenly across the sentences a bot produces.** Most cost nothing. A refund percentage costs whatever a customer can hold you to.

cells.c-use: Internal tools — a RAG chatbot over your own Jira tickets, for your own team
cells.c-dont: Client-facing answers on money, refunds or policy — a high chance of something that lands you in trouble

cells.c-use: Cases where the reader can sanity-check the answer — a teacher asking for questions on a chapter she already knows
cells.c-dont: Anything financially binding. "Quoting project quotations — never do this"

cells.c-use: Broad-coverage internal Q&A where you actively want web grounding as a fallback
THE RULE UNDERNEATH — there is a competent reader downstream who would spot a wrong answer. Dify is fine when a verification layer exists after it
cells.c-dont: The asker cannot check. The whole reason they are asking is that they don't know — so they take what they are given

ops.title: Why a stricter prompt doesn't close it

ops.markdown:
The verdict in the notes: **"This is solvable through stricter system prompt."** True as far as it goes — add *"use exact terms and numbers from the knowledge base"* and it stops some cases.

Then the ceiling:

> "The problem then becomes, how many system prompts can you actually fix that it will take care of all the scenarios?"

Every prompt fix is written against a failure you have **already seen**. Wrong-number-paraphrase is now covered; the next failure is one you haven't imagined, and you find out about it the way you found out about this one — from a consultant forwarding a screenshot.

**Prompt fixes are reactive by construction, and the failure surface is unbounded.** That is why the lecture needs a second tool — not because Dify is bad, but because "add another instruction" does not converge.

cells.c-w: A node holding cards. A card can be text, video, image, execute code, generate content, browse a page, capture information, insert a record
An embedded LLM you can query, plus exit conditions. The exit conditions are what make the flow non-linear

A standard node is a script — it runs the cards you put in it, in order. An autonomous node is a small agent — it has a model inside and it decides. Mixing them on one canvas is exactly the "you decide where the model may improvise" property
Left sidebar → Documents → drag and drop all files at once. No per-file settings — easier than Dify's one-at-a-time upload

Built-in persistence. Typed columns, rows written from a node. This is what turns a question-answering surface into a data-capture instrument — ALWAYS CAPTURE finally has somewhere for the answer to go
A card's result stored into a workflow variable (workflow.phone_number) and read by later nodes. Use string, not number — a numeric column cannot hold +91

ops.label: Start
Autonomous node — the LLM redirector
ops.detail: Holds the Dify system prompt plus one line: if the question is about refund, cancellation or an angry customer, a separate flow handles it — do not respond. Exit conditions are declared as detected intent.

ops.label: Answer from the KB, wait for the next question
Text card — the exact refund slab, 90 / 50 / 25
ops.detail: Not generated. Typed by a human once and returned verbatim every time. It cannot be paraphrased because nothing is composing it. This is the direct fix for the "most of his money back" failure.

ops.label: Text card — de-escalate
ops.detail: His copy was "Brother, calm down", which he flagged himself: never use terms like these in a production chatbot, it further aggravates the client — and a student pointed out it is gender-biased.

ops.label: Capture information → workflow.phone_number
Insert record → "angry clients" table
ops.detail: The number sits under Tables for someone to call back. This is hard rule 4 of the Dify prompt — "I'm getting a human on this right now" — upgraded from a promise into a mechanism that leaves a row behind.

ops.label: End
intent: cancellation / refund
intent: dissatisfaction / anger
neither

ops.markdown:
The Botpress system prompt is the Dify one **plus one line**:

> "If the question is about refund, cancellation or an angry customer, it will be handled by a separate flow — **do not respond.**"

Not *be careful with them*, not *quote exactly*. The model is **forbidden** from the topics that carry money and liability. Dify's prompt tried to make the model handle refunds correctly and got vague compliance; this one tells the model refunds are not its job.

**The model is still in the loop — doing a smaller job.** Intent detection is itself a model call: the LLM classifies what the user wants and picks the exit. So the model has been demoted from *composing the answer* to *choosing the branch*.

That is a much smaller failure surface. A misroute sends someone to the wrong text card and is recoverable. A mis-composed refund number is not.

ops.title: Why not Gems, and why not build it yourself

ops.markdown:
| Gemini Gems | These tools |
|---|---|
| Sticks to the knowledge base, and only the knowledge base — no choice | You choose whether to consult the KB, when, and what happens on each branch |
| No embeddable chat surface for your own site | Full preview and embed URL for your own site, your data, your configuration |

**On building it yourself:**

> "It is 100% possible to do that. The complexity of building this on your own would be probably 50× compared to how this is. Creating a workflow like this would not be possible. Having so many cards as options would not be possible. Having these tables would not be possible."

What you are buying is the workflow engine, the card palette and the tables — not the model.

**Deploy:** Publish changes → Embed → an iframe script tag you paste into any page.

ops.label: A different problem — not a failure of Botpress
ops.detail: §3 → §4 was a fix. §4 → §5 is not. Onboarding 20 freelance guides is a new problem, and reading it as "the more reliable tool" is the easiest way to misremember what Voiceflow is for.

ops.label: Same explanations and the same FAQ, every season
Internal users — who can sanity-check
ops.detail: By the competent-reader test this is exactly where Dify would be fine. So the reason to reach for Voiceflow is not reliability.

ops.label: Bad network — a guide standing at a trekking point in Kashmir
ops.detail: "Would you expect them to go to a website, fill a form and get a response? Especially read through your rules and regulations?" This constraint points at voice, and Voiceflow does chat and voice.

ops.label: The differentiator is organisational, not technical
ops.detail: Botpress already had a canvas. What is new is that the artifact is readable by someone who knows nothing about AI — which is why the tool shows up in conversation-designer and CX job descriptions rather than developer ones.

ops.markdown:
Voiceflow generated **six** of them from one paragraph of description, unasked.

A playbook is a **plain-prose document** containing: the questions to ask first, the deliverables to produce, the tools it may use, and the conditions under which it hands off to another playbook.

Two definitions, both accepted, and they do different work:

- **"A system prompt for Voiceflow — not just the system prompt but everything Voiceflow will do."** Tells you what it *is*: instructions in natural language.
- **"A function-based role description."** Tells you how to *scope* one: write a playbook per job, not per topic.

**One playbook can hand off to another**, and that is what replaces node-drawing:

> "You do not have to create the entire workflow any more… if the guide has a problem about some policies, transfer them to some other playbook. That playbook will be responsible for only handling the complaints. No need to create nodes then."

The canvas survives but is thin — drag a playbook block on, connect Start to it, done. Configuration happens by **editing the playbook's text**.

Botpress moved control up the dial by making you **draw** branches. Voiceflow keeps the control and changes the **medium**: the routing Botpress expresses as an exit condition on a canvas, Voiceflow expresses as a sentence inside a prose document.

It is the same architectural decision, written in a form a non-engineer can read and argue with. That is what "the canvas is a document a whole team can read" means in practice.

He proved it by running the agent, letting it ask its four opening questions, and asking the class how they would find out what happens next. **Answer: go read the playbook.**

In Botpress the answer to that question is "trace the canvas" — which a marketing lead cannot do.

ops.label: Tools toggle at two levels — and inheritance runs one way
A tool enabled at the agent level cannot be disabled inside a playbook
ops.detail: Turn it off at the agent first; then each playbook can enable or disable it independently. Tools here means knowledge base, buttons, cards, web search — and later APIs, functions and MCPs, which were named but deferred to a later class.

ops.label: Agent level is a floor, not a default
ops.detail: This is a permissions model, not a convenience setting.

ops.label: Safe habit: off at the agent, on per playbook
ops.detail: Least privilege applied to tool access. Get it backwards and you have a playbook searching the web when you thought you had disabled it.

ops.label: What it buys: playbooks with different capabilities
ops.detail: "Some with web search enabled, some without, some with API tools added, some with functions, MCPs added."

ops.markdown:
> "Your credits will expire and your credits will exhaust quicker than you potentially even know. That's one thing you have to be worried about when you use Voiceflow."

On screen: **$1** of total free credit — "the lowest of the credit points you get" — with $0.21 already spent.

Of the three, Voiceflow is the one he named as the most expensive.

cells.c-sit: Quick to set up, wide variety of questions, internal users who can sanity-check an answer
cells.c-why: Fastest to a working FAQ bot. You can even enable web grounding as a fallback when the KB doesn't cover it

cells.c-sit: Client-facing, and some answers are financially or legally binding
cells.c-why: Deterministic branches return the same vetted text every time. Money never passes through a generated sentence

cells.c-sit: You want that control, but you are not the only person who has to approve it
cells.c-why: The canvas is a shared readable artifact. Founders, consultants, marketing and CX can review and sign off before build effort is spent

ops.title: Reader, sentence, org — the three questions

ops.label: Each row is selected by a different question — ask them in this order
ops.detail: Compare the three on any single criterion and you will always conclude Voiceflow wins, which is the wrong answer. The rows are not ranked; they are three different tests.

ops.label: 1. The reader — can whoever receives this answer tell if it is wrong?
ops.detail: The competent-reader test. It is what makes Dify viable rather than reckless.

ops.label: 2. The sentence — does any answer commit the business to something?
ops.detail: If yes, that specific answer has to stop being generated.

ops.label: 3. The org — who has to say yes before this ships?
ops.detail: If the answer is "just me", Voiceflow's differentiator buys nothing and costs money. If it is the founder, CX and marketing, it buys the thing nothing else offers.

ops.label: This is the thesis made operational
ops.detail: "Match the shape of the tool to the shape of the risk" is a slogan until you can name the risks. Now you can: an unverifiable reader, a binding sentence, an unaligned team. Each row is one risk with the tool that absorbs it — so "which is best" is a malformed question.

ops.title: The choice is per answer type, not per bot

ops.markdown:
The binding-sentence question is asked of **answers**, not of products. The same bot can be perfectly safe describing a trekking route and unsafe quoting a cancellation slab.

Which is why the **mixed architecture** is the sensible shape rather than a compromise: autonomous for most of the conversation, scripted for the three sentences that actually commit you.

Picking a tool per bot is what makes the choice feel like a ranking. Picking per answer type is what makes it a design.

ops.title: The two trade-offs, and each tool's ceiling

ops.markdown:
**Voiceflow looks best but is the most expensive** of the three. Pair that with its credit warning: the tool that photographs best in a demo is the one whose free tier runs out fastest.

**Botpress gives the most control, but control means node handling.** You own every branch — a cost paid continuously, because every new edge case is a new branch someone has to draw and maintain.

Each ceiling sits opposite the other's:

- **Dify** — prompt fixes are reactive and do not converge
- **Botpress** — branches do not come free
- **Voiceflow** — the review loop and the price are both real overheads

And the blunt version, on Dify: *"If money runs on these, then I'd not recommend it."*

ops.title: Quiz 1 — why binding answers go in a deterministic branch

ops.markdown:
**Correct:** a generated answer is **probabilistic** — it can be phrased differently or wrongly on any given run, so you can never guarantee the exact figure. A deterministic branch returns the same vetted text every single time.

The three wrong options were all **capability** claims — too slow, can't read a KB, doesn't work on messaging channels — and every one is factually false. The right answer is not a capability claim at all; it is about **variance**.

*Carry that pattern:* when the subject is reliability, the answer is usually about consistency across runs, not about what the system can or cannot do.

> "An LLM can be considered to be a five-year-old kid. You teach them Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, you sing it to them. But when a guest comes over and you ask them to sing it — they might or might not. That probability of *may or may not* is the same with an LLM."

The analogy is precise: the child **knows** the song. Capability is not in question — performance on a given occasion is. Which is exactly the paraphrase failure: the model had the document and the number, and on that run said "most of his money".

ops.title: Quiz 2 — what a design canvas buys a team

ops.markdown:
**Correct:** a shared, readable artifact that non-engineers can review, critique and approve **before build effort is spent**.

A flow builder gives you a working prototype, and a good one — but it is not shareable. Hand that canvas to someone in marketing and they can do nothing with it; *"this will write the phone number in the table and this will happen"* is too complicated to follow. The design artifact can go to a CEO, CTO, VP, marketing or sales, who can comment, attach documents and request changes.

The load-bearing phrase is **before build effort is spent**. A prototype proves the thing works; it does not help you find out you built the wrong thing. Review only saves anything if it happens upstream of the build — which is why this is a design-time property, not a runtime one.

ops.label: 900 conversations × 6 messages = 5,400 messages a month
ops.detail: Every message triggers an LLM call. That clause is the whole question — people estimate against conversations, and the meter runs on messages.

ops.label: What bites first: message and credit volume
ops.detail: 5,400 blows past every free tier well inside the first week. The seat limit doesn't bite — you are the only builder. The agent cap doesn't bite — you don't need more than two.

ops.label: Free tiers fit roughly 200–700 conversations a month
ops.detail: "A bakery, something that does not usually rely on chatbots." A product needing heavy chat has to go paid.

ops.label: Why only 54% got it — it is a modelling question, not a recall one
ops.detail: You have to convert conversations to messages, know each message is a billable call, then check that number against three different units — credits, messages, interaction credits. Two of the four options are true statements about free tiers that are irrelevant to this business.

ops.label: The transferable move: when pricing a bot, count messages and multiply
ops.detail: Conversations are the unit the client thinks in, and the unit that under-counts by 6×.

ops.title: The page and the bot are decoupled

ops.markdown:
In the closing demo, Cursor generated a static HTML site for the travel company and the chat bubble on it was the Botpress agent — connected by **one script tag** and nothing else.

> "Now where is this chat happening? This is happening on Botpress. I have not coded this."

The architectural point: the website and the agent share no code, no build and no deployment. Which means **the bot is portable** — it drops onto any page, on any site, with no integration work.

That is what "deploy to many channels from one build" looks like in practice, and it is why the embed snippet is the deliverable rather than the bot's internals.

Two defects he flagged in his own generated page: a rupee sign that rendered as `?` (an encoding problem), and an emergency contact number that was **invented** — *"I have no idea whose number this is."*

The second is the whole lecture arriving in the demo. Nobody asked for an emergency contact. The agent produced one because the page seemed to need it and nothing in the folder supplied it.

**An unrequested, unverifiable, plausible detail, sitting in a client-facing artifact.** Same failure family as "most of his money back" — different tool, different surface, identical shape.

The generalisation worth keeping: generated artifacts invent most freely in the gaps *you did not specify*, because that is where nothing contradicts them. Review the parts you never asked for first.

*(He also showed that a student's AI Studio login page was fake — any password unlocked it — and accepted that a prototype is allowed to be.)*

ops.title: A KB is the unit of scoping, not a file

ops.markdown:
*"Can I select which files to consider — two of the four?"* Not directly. Either **split into two knowledge bases**, or instruct the retrieval step in the prompt to use only those files.

Prefer separate KBs, because **disabling a file disables it everywhere that KB is used**. File-level toggling is a global switch wearing the costume of a local one.

So scope at the knowledge-base boundary: if two agents need different slices of the same folder, that is two knowledge bases, not one with selective files.

ops.title: Data security is verified, not assumed

ops.markdown:
*"Is my data secure when I upload it?"*

The vendors handle data well, encryption and privacy policies apply on the **free tier too**, and your data is not used for training.

But the operative half of the answer is the second half: **check the vendor's customer feedback and GDPR compliance against your client's requirements before choosing.**

That is the honest form — not "it is safe", but *safety is a per-client requirement you verify, not a property you assume*. Different clients draw the line in different places, and the line is theirs to draw.

Pairs with self-hosting: when a client's answer is that nothing may leave their premises, an open-source tool you can host yourself is the only option still standing.

cells.c-q: Isn't this the same as n8n?
cells.c-b: They look alike — all node-based workflow builders. n8n is better for email and marketing automation; these are better for chatbots

cells.c-q: Can I just build chatbots in Claude?
cells.c-b: Claude is the LLM layer. The knowledge base, prompt routing and integration are what these three tools provide — Claude can be the API endpoint underneath. The model is a component, not the product

cells.c-q: Can I link Confluence as a knowledge base?
cells.c-b: Yes — URLs and connectors, not just file upload. It changes the maintenance story: a connected source updates, an uploaded file goes stale

cells.c-q: Will we learn API and MCP integration with these?
